During this course, various aspects of the reality of our country have been analysed and have been shown to be the important ones that have been changed. With this background, I will make some comments on some aspects that have to be taken into account in relation to the relationship between our country and our economy and the activities of the European Central Bank (ECB). Spain AND THE NEW PODERING EUROPEAN Monetary System A new monetary order has been introduced in Spain and the European Union since 1990. This important institutional and functional change has been based on two steps in the right line: firstly the depolitisation of monetary power by granting the European Bank's autonomy (1994) and then the decentralization and supranationalization of the euro area (the euro area's currency) as a whole. The supranationalisation of the European monetary power is, of course, the consequence of the establishment of the euro as a single European currency, which has replaced, by advantage, the old peseta and the remaining nine currencies of the euro area member countries. A single currency involves the improvement of the single market and therefore the process of economic integration of the European economy and, more importantly, means a path along the way towards the European Union. The possible disadvantages that the introduction of the euro may have to represent the Spanish and European citizens in the order of practice must be compared with these high objectives of the euro area, which the euro option leads to. The Bank of Spain, as well as the national central banks of the other ten countries integrated into the new economic area, has become part of a small-scale It can be said that the ECB is generally responsible for the functions of decision-making, coordination and guaranteeing the performance of the functions entrusted to the ESCB, while the rest of the general functions of the system, such as the provision of information or execution of operations, are carried out decentralisedly, in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity, by the national central banks (NCB), in our case by the Bank of Spain. The Bank of Spain is therefore an institution of great importance in the economic administration of Spain. Such coordination, in addition to the Council of Government and the General Council, takes place in the said Committees, composed of experts from the NCBs and the ECB, whose mandates cover the various areas of the system's activities (statistics, payment system, operations, tickets, etc.) and carry out an important preparatory work prior to considering the different matters in the Executive Committee. THE SECB's Monetary Policy PUBLIC PUBLIC APPLICATION The ECB's approach to monetary policy presents some differences with respect to the Bank of Spain as regards the instruments available to the central bank and in the procedures followed in the use of monetary regulation instruments. In this context, the existence of the two permanent facilities, the credit margin and the deposit margin, allows the discretion of the banking or counterparty entities to obtain credit for one day or to deposit liquidity surpluses, thus reducing the need to make adjustments to the short term less than the regular operations of financing and eliminating the practice of carrying out exceptional and discretionary operations to credit institutions against market fraud. The differences between the monetary policy of the Eurosystem and the Bank of Spain are partly due to the different nature of the cash rate applied in both cases. The former cash ratio of the Bank of Spain has a much shorter time frame and a shorter time interval between the cash flow rate and the coverage period, resulting in a higher rate of interest rates at a given time, unless the Bank of Spain is less active in the market than the current rate of cash flow. In this way, the cash coefficient ceases to be a source of monetary income for the central bank and therefore a cost for the banks, which allows them to compete on equal terms with the banks of the systems where they are not required, without prejudice to the basic purpose of the coefficient which is to maintain liquidity conditions and increase the effectiveness of monetary policy. In the face of the usual practice of the Bank of Spain to carry out variable substations, the SEBC has so far carried out in its main financing operations of fixed-type subsidised types with a fixed amount, in which the counterparty entities are set up by the amount of liquidity with which they want to operate to the type of interest established by the ECB and are only offering the amount required by the monetary policy requirements by applying it in the form of the requested volume. On the other hand, to the extent that the ECB's monetary policy focuses on its operational objective of directing the type of interbank interest to a given level of intervention, the possibility of obtaining liquidity in the market in the short term instead of in the monetary substations is reduced. This substation procedure is used by the ESCB in short-term financing operations, monthly frequency and quarterly windings, which inject around 30% of the liquidity provided by the Eurosystem.
